source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang, Mausam (2023) Adaptive-Consistency: stopping rule and its own stated limit (re-read, gap 1)
finding: The Beta stop rule asks only whether the leading answer is ahead of the runner-up. It never asks whether the leading answer is right. The authors list a related limit. Accuracy is always compared with Self-Consistency at 40 samples, so a wrong consensus that SC-40 also reaches is not counted as a stopping error.
numbers: Stop when P(p1 > p2) from Beta(v1+1, v2+1) passes Cthresh=0.95. By my own arithmetic, 4 unanimous votes give 1-0.5^5 = 0.969 and stop; 3 give 0.9375 and do not. Table 1: 3.3x fewer samples on maths (accuracy 73.2 vs 73.1), 2.9x commonsense (66.0 vs 65.8), 3.8x symbolic (72.8 vs 72.8), 2.4x code (35.2 vs 35.6); 17 datasets, 3 models.
quote: any limitations or biases in the LLM would persist in the Adaptive-Consistency
limits: The 4-vote figure is my derivation from the stated formula, not a number printed in the paper. No count of early-stopped items that were wrong. Limitations section admits the criterion may trigger when the majority is not stable, and that LLM biases persist.
agent_relevance: Stability stopping is a rule for matching SC-40, not for being right. Its error floor is the error floor of SC.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Adaptive-Consistency, per-model results (gap 7)
finding: A weaker model saves much less than a stronger one under the same fixed 0.95 threshold, because its samples disagree longer. The agreement rule adapts to model strength on its own, without a model-specific threshold.
numbers: Table 1: GPT-3.5-Turbo 40 -> 10.0 generations (4.4x, accuracy 76.4 -> 76.2). Vicuna-13B 40 -> 21.7 (1.9x, 54.0 -> 54.1). Code-davinci-002 104.1 -> 49.4 (3.4x, 69.7 -> 69.8). Boolean Expressions 7.9x; SVAMP under 5 samples on average.
limits: Three models only, all 2023 era, all with a 40-sample cap. No reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Agreement-based stopping already scales with model strength through the vote. A confidence gate (ReASC, d07) does not, and needs its threshold set per model.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Adaptive-Consistency, Section 5.3 stop-function comparison (gap 6)
finding: The nearest thing to a value-of-computation test: Bayesian stability criteria beat simple vote-share rules at equal cost. BETA, Dirichlet and Chinese-restaurant-process (Monte Carlo 'stability of the current majority') were similar. A raw MAJORITY-threshold rule did worst apart from RANDOM. No criterion prices an extra sample or models the expected change of the leading answer.
numbers: GSM-8K: at an average of 10 samples Adaptive-Consistency is about 3% more accurate than Self-Consistency at the same cost. Dirichlet and CRP are about four orders of magnitude slower than Beta but still negligible next to LLM inference.
limits: Figures read as text only. No exact per-point numbers from Appendix C.2 Table 7 (not opened). Myopic VOC with a cost term was not tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open. The evidence says use a posterior over the leading answer, not a vote-share threshold.

source: Brown, Juravsky, Ehrlich, Clark, Le, Re, Mirhoseini (2024) Large Language Monkeys, Section 4.1 and Figure 8 (gaps 1 and 10)
finding: With a perfect checker, extra samples keep paying. With agreement or a reward model they stop paying after about 100 samples. Many problems are solved only by rare samples while the common answer is wrong, so agreement would stop on the wrong answer. Figure 8 shows these problems (bars red where the majority answer was wrong).
numbers: MATH, Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000. Majority vote or reward-model selection moves only from 40.50% to 41.41% over that range. ArmoRM reward model. Over 90% of 105 hand-graded correct GSM8K chains of thought were faithful, so a verifier has signal to use.
quote: majority voting and reward models plateau beyond several hundred samples
limits: Maths only. Large sample counts, not the 4-16 range where stopping rules work. The pass@k gap is a ceiling for a perfect checker, not a measured stop-on-pass rule.
agent_relevance: If a real checker exists, agreement is a poor stand-in for it. The gap between 41% and 98% is the room for a checker-based stop.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys, Section 4.2: verifier imperfections (gap 10)
finding: Even code checkers are not clean. Stopping on a checker pass inherits false positives and false negatives.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: 11.3% of problems have flaky test suites that sometimes fail even the gold patch. CodeContests: of 122 test problems with Python 3 reference solutions, 35 have a listed correct solution that fails the tests.
limits: These are benchmark-quality findings. The share of false passes was not given.
agent_relevance: A stop-on-pass rule needs a checker whose false-pass rate is known. Otherwise it is only as good as the test suite.

source: Kim, Garg, Peng, Garg (2025) Correlated Errors in Large Language Models (gap 1, indirect)
finding: Different models share their mistakes. When two models are both wrong they pick the same wrong answer far more often than chance. Samples from one model should correlate even more, which is the failure case for agreement-based stopping.
numbers: Mean agreement when both models are wrong: 0.423 on HuggingFace Open LLM Leaderboard MMLU data (349 models, 12,032 questions; chance about 0.12) and about 0.60 on HELM (71 models, 14,042 questions; chance 1/3). 100% of pairs beat chance on HuggingFace and 97.5% on HELM. Extreme pair 0.9987.
quote: models agree 60% of the time when both models err
limits: Across models, not repeated samples from one model. Multiple-choice data. Page read through a page-extraction tool; the last 17k characters were not read. Chance values partly garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Shared wrong answers are common. Agreement cannot separate 'known' from 'confidently wrong' without a second signal.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Reliability-Aware Adaptive Self-Consistency (ReASC), Table 2: accuracy of accepted single samples (gaps 1 and 7)
finding: Stage 1 accepts one sample when its confidence passes a gate. The accepted answers are not all right, and the share accepted depends strongly on model strength and task. This is the only direct measure of error among early-stopped items found.
numbers: Offline gate, accepted share / accuracy of accepted: GSM8K Llama-3.2-3B 48.98% / 91.33%, Gemma-3-4B 51.18% / 97.78%, Qwen-2.5-7B 59.59% / 97.58%, Gemma-3-27B 60.58% / 98.62%. MATH500: Llama-3.2-3B 7.2% / 86.11%, Gemma-3-4B 34.0% / 96.47%, Qwen-2.5-7B 38.4% / 91.67%, Gemma-3-27B 36.6% / 97.27%. Online gate GSM8K: 28.1-40.6% accepted at 93.5-99.4% accuracy.
limits: The gate is set from a target accuracy on calibration data, so the wrong-accept rate (1.4% to 8.7% on GSM8K, 2.7% to 13.9% on MATH500) is partly a design choice. Confidence gate, not vote stability. Maths and GPQA only. No unanimity-on-wrong count.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: acceptance rose with model size on both sets (GSM8K 49% to 61%, MATH500 7% to 37%), so one confidence threshold does not give one stop point. Set the gate from a target accuracy on calibration items, per model.

source: Kim et al. (2026) ReASC, Table 1: cost against a fixed 16-sample baseline (gap 5)
finding: Against 16 samples, not 40, the savings of ESC and ASC are smaller and sometimes tiny on hard sets. ReASC adds more saving. Costs are in TFLOPs, so prompt reading is presumably counted.
numbers: Llama-3.2-3B, ESC (window 4) vs SC k=16: GSM8K -44.6%, MATH500 -15.4%, Omni-Math -4.4%, GPQA-Diamond -15.4%. Gemma-3-27B GSM8K: ESC -71.4%, ReASC offline -82.4%, online -78.8%; MATH500 ESC -56.6%, ReASC -65.2%. Accuracy within 0.2 on most cells, e.g. Gemma-3-27B GSM8K 97.04 for SC, ESC and ReASC online; Qwen-2.5-7B GSM8K ReASC offline 94.09 vs SC 94.31.
limits: Same-author method against baselines it re-implemented. TFLOP accounting of prompts not checked in the text. Savings against k=16 range from 4% to 82% by model and set.
agent_relevance: Weak models on hard sets get almost nothing from vote stopping (Omni-Math 3B -4.4%). Plan budget for the hard tail, not the average.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Difficulty-Adaptive Self-Consistency (DSC), Tables 1-4: total cost with input tokens (gap 5)
finding: When each extra round re-sends the prompt, ASC and ESC can cost more than plain SC. The few-shot prompt is long, so input cost dominates. This is the strongest evidence that output-only sample counts overstate savings.
numbers: GSM8K Table 1: GPT-4 input 846.3 tokens vs output 142.1 per call; GPT-3.5 846.3 vs 163.7. Table 4, Mistral-7B-Instruct on GSM8K, SC-40: input 846, output 6,045, cost 0.3881; ASC input 15,982, output 3,265, cost 0.6754 (+74%); ESC input 4,458, output 4,415, cost 0.3986 (+3%); DSC input 1,617, output 3,857, cost 0.2799 (-28%). GPT-4 MATH Table 2: SC-40 0.4220, ASC 0.5726, ESC 0.4062, DSC 0.3142. Table 3 (max 16 samples): SC 0.1791, ESC 0.1870, DSC 0.1659.
limits: The DSC authors built the comparison and their method wins. Prices are API prices. With prompt caching or n-sampling in one call the input penalty largely disappears, so this is the worst case.
agent_relevance: Sample all needed answers in one call per round where possible and cache the prompt. If rounds re-send the context, count input tokens before claiming a saving.

source: Damani, Shenfeld, Peng, Bobu, Andreas (2024) Learning How Hard to Think (gaps 3 and 9)
finding: A small probe on the model's hidden states predicts how much extra samples will help, and allocates a budget per question. Prediction accuracy is only moderate, and its errors can wreck online allocation. The same predictor routes between two decoding procedures or two models.
numbers: Probes trained on 128 samples per training query (maths). Median-split accuracy of the predictor: Code 74%, Math 84%, Chat model routing 72%, Chat value-augmented routing 72%. Best-of-k: up to 50% less compute on Math and Code at equal success, up to 10% on Chat (25-40% with the tranches variant). Routing: 25-40% fewer calls to the expensive decoder (value-augmented sampling) at similar reward; Gemma-2B/7B and sampling vs value-augmented sampling matched the strong decoder while calling it 50-75% of the time. On code the online variant fell BELOW plain best-of-k at high budget (B>=8): a true 0% pass rate predicted as 1% attracts a large budget. 50% of code problems have zero success probability; 5% on Math.
limits: The 128 samples per question are needed once for training, not per test question. Oracle verifiers for maths and code, reward model for chat. 2024 models (Mathstral-7B, Gemma, Llama-7B). Routing between think and no-think was not tested.
agent_relevance: Difficulty can be learned from the question text, but treat the predictor as noisy: bin coarsely and cap per-question budgets.

source: Manvi, Singh, Ermon (2024) Adaptive Inference-Time Compute: LLMs can predict if they can do better (gaps 3, 5, 10)
finding: One extra token after a draft answer ('would you do better if you started over?') gives a probability that resampling will beat the draft. Using it to decide whether to resample beats a fixed small sample count, and beats the underlying reward model as a stop signal.
numbers: Llama 3.1 8B on GSM8K, Best-of-N with the self-evaluation selector: 84.2% at 1 sample, 87.7% at 2, 88.9% at 4, 89.9% at 8, 91.0% at 16 (share of max gain 0, 51.5, 69.1, 83.8, 100). Adaptive threshold 0.92 with temperature annealing: 89.2% using 1.2 samples on average (73.5% of the gain). Threshold 0.98 with annealing: 90.8% at 3.7 samples (97.1%); without annealing 4.1 samples. Fixed best-of-4 gets 69.1% of the gain. With the reward model as the stop signal: 86.9% to 89.9% at 1.4 to 6.9 samples, which the authors say is no better than random selection. AlpacaEval win rate vs GPT-4 21% to 34% at 16 samples. Early pruning drops 50-75% of samples.
limits: One model family, GSM8K and AlpacaEval, trained on LMSYS-derived preferences. The stop head still needs training data. 'Samples' counts completions, not input tokens.
agent_relevance: Compare with a small fixed baseline (4), not 16: 1.2 samples adaptive beats 4 fixed on GSM8K. A self-asked 'would redoing improve this' check is a cheap stop signal worth testing at prompt level, with the training caveat.

source: My calculation: pass-rate estimate quality from 1-16 samples (gap 3; labelled as a model, not a measurement)
finding: Simulated per-question pass rate p drawn from three Beta priors; n samples per question. Four samples rank easy against hard about as well as the learned probe in d10. Five-way bins stay noisy until about 16 samples. So routing by a coarse easy/hard class needs 2-4 samples, but Snell-style five bins do not.
numbers: 400,000 simulated questions. Median-split accuracy (easy vs hard half), U-shape Beta(.5,.5): n=1 0.82, n=2 0.82, n=4 0.87, n=8 0.91, n=16 0.94. Uniform Beta(1,1): 0.75, 0.75, 0.81, 0.86, 0.90. Mostly-easy Beta(2,.7): 0.62, 0.71, 0.79, 0.84, 0.88. Exact quintile match: n=4 0.40-0.52, n=16 0.61-0.75. Mean absolute error of the pass rate: n=4 0.13-0.16, n=16 0.06-0.08.
limits: Pure simulation: independent samples, fixed per-question pass rate, Beta prior. Real pass-rate distributions differ. Not a literature result; Snell's bins were not re-estimated. Compare with d10 (learned probe 72-84%).
agent_relevance: Cheap difficulty from 2-4 samples is good enough for a two- or three-way route. The first samples are not wasted if they also feed the vote.

source: My calculation: how many early-stopped items are wrong when 4 samples agree (gap 1; labelled as a model)
finding: The share of wrong items among those stopped at 4 unanimous votes depends on how concentrated the wrong answers are and on task difficulty. If errors are scattered, wrong stops are rare. If one wrong answer holds most of the error mass, they are common. Real data on that concentration is the missing measurement.
numbers: 2,000,000 simulated questions, 4 unanimous votes to stop. Top wrong answer holds share w of the wrong mass. Uniform pass rate: w=1.0 gives 50% of stopped items wrong; w=0.7 19%; w=0.5 6%; w=0.3 0.8%. Easy-skewed Beta(2,.7): 9%, 2.3%, 0.6%, 0.1%. Hard-skewed Beta(.7,1.5): 83%, 54%, 24%, 4%. Share of items that stop at all ranges 8% to 55%.
limits: Simulation under iid sampling and one dominant wrong answer. No dataset behind w. Brown et al. Figure 8 (d04) and Kim et al. (d06) suggest w is not small on hard items.
agent_relevance: Do not trust vote-stability to catch confidently-wrong items on hard questions. Add an independent signal (a checker, or a differently-prompted sample) before stopping.

source: Kang, Deng, Xiao, Mo, Lee, Bing (2025) First Try Matters: Revisiting the role of reflection in reasoning models (gap 4)
finding: Reflection after the first candidate answer is mostly confirmation. Few items flip from wrong to right. Most of the accuracy comes from the first candidate. This reconciles 'more thinking helps' (small gain) with 'longer chains are worse within a question' (long ones are the hard or wrong ones).
numbers: Eight reasoning models, five maths sets (AIME24, AIME25, AMC, OlympiadBench, MATH500). Over 90% of reflections are confirmatory; wrong-to-right 'mostly less than 2%'. Average first-candidate vs final accuracy: MiMo-7B-RL 78.8 vs 81.2; R1-Distill-Qwen-7B 61.5 vs 64.4; R1-Distill-Llama-8B 62.3 vs 65.1; Qwen3-8B 81.2 vs 84.7; R1-0528-Qwen3-8B 79.8 vs 81.4; gpt-oss-20b 79.3 vs 82.4; Magistral-Small 82.0 vs 85.0; R1-0528 89.1 vs 90.6. Reflections use 16.8-47.8% of tokens for 1.4-3.5 points. Qwen3-8B early stop: baseline 84.7% at 15,125 tokens; candidate detector alone -29.9% tokens, -3.8 points; with a question-aware controller -24.5% tokens (11,414) at 81.8% (-2.9 points). Training with more reflections: +4.05 overall, of which +3.75 from first-answer accuracy and +0.3 from reflection.
quote: reflections are predominantly confirmatory and rarely alter the model's initial answer
limits: Read through a page-extraction tool, not the PDF. The right-to-wrong rate is in a figure and was not retrievable. This is natural reflection, not forced 'Wait'. Maths only. A paired split of a forced re-check by first-answer correctness is still not given.
agent_relevance: Stopping at the first candidate costs 1.5-3.5 points and saves a quarter to a third of tokens on maths. Forced re-check is worth it where the first answer is uncertain, not by default.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024, ICLR) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (gaps 4 and 10)
finding: Asking the same model to re-check its answer, with no outside label, tends to lower accuracy. The same re-check with an oracle label that says when to stop gives large gains. This is the paired result for a prompted re-check: the gain is in knowing when to stop, which the model cannot do alone.
numbers: GSM8K, GPT-3.5: 75.9 standard, 75.1 after round 1, 74.7 after round 2. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0. CommonSenseQA GPT-3.5 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8. HotpotQA GPT-3.5 26.0 -> 25.0 -> 25.0; GPT-4 49.0 -> 49.0 -> 43.0. With oracle labels (stop when correct): GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 95.5, GPT-4 95.5 -> 97.5, GPT-4 HotpotQA 49 -> 59. GPT-3.5 kept its first answer 74.7% of the time on GSM8K, and changed correct to incorrect more often than the reverse.
limits: 2023 chat models, not reasoning models. Prompted critique, not 'Wait'. Small test samples (percentages in the figure are of 200 questions on some sets).
agent_relevance: A re-check needs an outside stop signal. With a checker, forced re-check is a large win. Without one, it can lose points.

source: Zhang, Chen, Pan, Zhao, Panda, Li, He (2025) Reasoning Models Know When They're Right: probing hidden states for self-verification (gaps 2 and 4)
finding: A trained probe on hidden states at each intermediate answer predicts whether that answer is right, well enough to stop on. This is a trained stopper for free-form reasoning, but it does not transfer across domains.
numbers: R1-Distill-Llama-8B on MATH, max 10K tokens: probe threshold 0.85 gives 88.2% (same as no early exit) with about 24% fewer tokens. Threshold 0.9 or more gives 88.6% (identical) with 19% fewer. At matched tokens it beats a static 'stop after m chunks' rule by up to 5 points (87.4% at 0.8 vs about 82.5%). In-distribution ROC-AUC above 0.7 and ECE below 0.1. Out of distribution: MATH to GSM8K 0.83, GSM8K to MATH 0.80; on AIME 0.69-0.81 with ECE 0.25-0.31; logic data KnowLogic 0.56-0.67.
limits: Needs training data from the same model and domain. The token saving is against the full trace capped at 10K. Single model on the headline test.
agent_relevance: Free-form stopping that works so far needs a trained component. See d17 for a prompt-only counter-example in agent loops.

source: Liu et al. (2025, v2) Budget-Aware Tool Use Enables Effective Agent Scaling: Budget Tracker (gap 2)
finding: For agent loops with no vote, a prompt-only signal exists: show the agent how much tool budget is left each turn. Without it, ReAct agents stop early and plateau. With it they use extra budget and cost less at equal accuracy. A hidden cap does not do this.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-Pro, BrowseComp, 3 runs: ReAct 12.6 at budget 100, 10.3 at budget 10, 10.5 at 30; with Budget Tracker at budget 10: 12.8, with 40.4% fewer search calls, 19.9% fewer browse calls, 31.3% lower cost. Table 1 gains: BrowseComp 12.6 -> 14.6, BrowseComp-ZH 31.5 -> 32.9, HLE-Search 20.5 -> 21.8. ReAct capped at 30.7% on BrowseComp-ZH for all budgets of 30 and up; BATS rose 29.8% (budget 3) to 37.4% (budget 200). SWE-bench Verified, budget 50: resolve rate 36.8% -> 55.4% with 46.0 vs 45.7 tool calls. Conversational subset: Avg@4 47.8 -> 55.5 at budget 10.
limits: The tracker is a counter shown to the agent, not a learned stop decision. Same authors for baseline and method. The main-table gains are small against run noise (BrowseComp +2.0 with +/-1.2). Gemini and Claude Sonnet 4 only.
agent_relevance: For loops, a visible turn counter is a cheap better-than-blind-cap baseline. Test it against a bare cap and against model-chosen stops (CaRT).

source: Liu et al. (2025) BATS: stop on first verified answer versus keep going (gaps 2 and 10)
finding: Stopping an agent at its first self-verified answer costs accuracy compared with spending the rest of the budget on new attempts. The model's own check is not strong enough to trust as a stop. The sequential forcing prompt used in the paper reads 'Wait, you still have remaining tool budget'.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-Pro, budget 100 per tool: BATS continuing after a verified answer 24.6% BrowseComp, 46.0% BrowseComp-ZH, 27.0% HLE-Search (Table 3). BATS with early stop at the first verified answer 18.7, 39.1, 23.0 (Table 4 ablation). Removing the verifier module: BrowseComp 18.7 -> 15.4.
limits: Verification is the model's own, not an external test. The early-stop and continue arms differ in total budget used. Numbers come from different sections of the paper.
agent_relevance: Stop-on-self-verified-pass is not strictly better than agreement: it loses 6-8 points here. Self-verification should be independent of the first attempt.

source: Pan, Zhang, Zhao, Han (2025) Route to Reason: Adaptive routing for LLM and reasoning strategy selection (gap 9)
finding: One router can pick both the model and the reasoning strategy, including the think versus no-think switch, from the question text. For Qwen3-4B it learns to turn thinking on only when needed.
numbers: Seven models and four strategies (vanilla, CoT, PAL, CoD), four tasks, 70/30 split. Overall: 82.5% accuracy at 1,091.3 tokens, +2.5 points and over 60% fewer tokens than the largest single model QwQ-32B; over 39.6% fewer tokens than EmbedLLM at equal or better accuracy. Out of distribution: 0.5 points above QwQ with 393.9 vs 1,387.3 tokens. Qwen3-4B Table 4: non-thinking 73.4% at 592.1 tokens; thinking 82.4% at 3,112.8; RouteLLM 82.8% at 2,247.1; EmbedLLM 83.2% at 2,623.5; KNN-Router 80.6% at 1,418.7; RTR 83.8% at 1,321.1 (-57.6% tokens vs always-thinking, +1.4 points). Token-length predictor: about 80% correct within 200 tokens for non-reasoning models, about 60% within 600 tokens for reasoning models.
limits: Authors' own baselines. Maths and MMLU-type tasks. The router needs trained performance and token predictors. Single-model selection only.
agent_relevance: Routing between think and no-think is competitive with routing between models, and one router can cover both axes. The saving is against always-think, not against a tuned stop rule.

source: Kim et al. (2026) ReASC, Appendix E: the DeepConf confidence signal reused by others (gap 8)
finding: An independent group reused DeepConf's bottom-10% group-confidence idea on small non-reasoning instruct models and found it separates correct from wrong better than whole-response confidence. This partly replicates the signal, not the DeepConf stop pipeline. No re-run of DSC by others turned up in the papers opened.
numbers: Gemma-3-4B-it on MATH: AUROC 0.860 for Bottom-10% group confidence, 0.823 average group, 0.801 response-level self-certainty, 0.699 tail group. Window size 128 gives 0.874 (Gemma-3-4B) and 0.744 (Qwen-2.5-3B); 32 gives 0.832 and 0.714; 768 gives 0.862 and 0.725.
limits: Only the signal was reused. No DeepConf online stopping or voting filter, no reasoning models, maths only. Citation lookups (Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex) were rate-limited, so the absence of other replications is unproven.
agent_relevance: The tail-confidence signal travels to other models. Gap 8 is not closed: the DeepConf token-saving claim and the DSC cost claim still rest on their own authors.

source: Huang, Huang, Leng, Liu, Huang (2025) Efficient Test-Time Scaling via Self-Calibration (gaps 3 and 10)
finding: Training a model to output a calibrated confidence in one forward pass lets sampling stop when one sample is confident enough. At a small budget, early stopping can stop too soon and plain Best-of-N does better.
numbers: Fig 1, MathQA, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct trained model: confidence-weighted SC reaches the accuracy of plain SC with 39.8%, 50.4% and 94.2% fewer samples at three accuracy levels. Budget 16: MathQA SC 81.0 vs SC with confidence 83.6; DeepSeek-R1-Distill 1.5B on ARC-challenge Best-of-N 58.9 vs early stop 66.5. GSM8K ECE 13.70 -> 3.79 with accuracy 77.44% -> 80.43%. Self-generated confidence is about as good as an equal-size reward model for Best-of-16 (Qwen MathQA 84.0 vs 82.1; Object Counting 72.0 vs 72.6).
quote: When the sample budget is small, Best-of-N performs better than early stopping
limits: Needs training on the target distribution (2,000 questions per dataset in the main setup). Savings in samples, not tokens. Small 2025 models.
agent_relevance: A calibrated one-pass confidence is a viable stop signal where there is no vote, but it needs training on the target distribution.
